blocks.text: You run a campaign, ten creators post, the comments section fills up and the views look good. Then someone asks which creator actually moved product and you have nothing to point to except a feeling.
That gap between activity and evidence is the whole problem with creator marketing measurement. This is how to track which creator content actually drives sales, instead of guessing from engagement.
How do you track which creator content actually drives sales?

You give every creator a unique link or discount code before they post anything, and you track orders back to that link or code rather than to the post itself. Likes, comments and views happen on the platform and never touch your store, so they cannot be matched to a Shopify order. A code or link can, because it travels with the customer from the content to checkout.

This has to be set up before the first post goes live. If a creator posts first and you hand them a code afterwards, you've already lost the sales that happened in that window, and you'll never know how many there were.
Why likes and views don't tell you anything about revenue

A video with a lot of views can sell nothing, and a video with modest views can sell steadily for weeks. Views measure reach. They don't measure intent, and they definitely don't measure whether someone opened a new tab, found your site and paid.

Engagement is a reasonable signal for whether a creator's audience likes the content style. It's a poor signal for revenue because comments and saves come from people who were already going to watch the video anyway, not necessarily from people who were going to buy. Brands that report on views and comments as if they were sales metrics usually find out later that the two numbers move independently of each other.

If you want a fuller picture of which metrics matter at each stage, [creator marketing KPIs for ecommerce, stage by stage](/blog/creator-marketing-kpis-for-ecommerce) covers what to watch before and after the sale happens.
How to set up unique links and codes before a campaign starts

Every creator in the campaign gets their own code or their own link, never a shared one. A shared code tells you the campaign worked in general. A unique code tells you which specific creator's audience bought, which is the number you actually need when deciding who to work with again.

Say you're running a gifted campaign for a coffee brand with a dozen creators posting brew tutorials. Each creator gets a code built from their handle, say a short variant they can say on camera easily. Orders using that code attribute straight back to them in your reporting, and at the end of the month you can see which two or three creators brought in most of the tracked sales and which ones brought in almost none, despite similar view counts.

On Shopify, affiliate sales are tracked through unique creator links and discount codes, with commission payouts handled through the platform, so the attribution and the payment sit in the same place instead of two spreadsheets that drift apart. If you're setting this up for the first time, [how to run a creator campaign on a Shopify store](/blog/run-creator-campaign-shopify-store) walks through the mechanics.
What to do when a creator posts organically without a code

This happens, and it's not a disaster if you catch it early. A creator you gifted product to posts on their own schedule, forgets to mention the code, or uses a general link instead of their own. The fix is to reach out immediately and ask them to add a pinned comment or edit the caption with their code, because most of the sales window for a single post happens in the first days it's live.

The better fix is prevention. Build the code into the brief itself as a non-negotiable line, not a suggestion buried at the bottom. If you're putting a brief together, [a creator brief template for ecommerce that stops reshoots](/blog/creator-brief-template-for-ecommerce) has a version of this built in.

It's also worth checking your codes aren't leaking outside the creator relationship entirely. A code that gets shared on a coupon site stops meaning anything about that creator's audience, which is covered in [the hidden cost of uncontrolled discount codes](/blog/leaked-discount-codes).
How to read the data once sales start coming in

Once codes are live, resist the urge to judge a creator after a single post. Look at tracked sales against the content delivered and the audience reached for that creator specifically, over the full length of the campaign, not the first day. Some creators convert slowly because their audience watches, thinks about it and buys a week later after seeing the product again somewhere else.

Linkable's reporting shows content delivered, audiences reached, engagement generated and tracked sales per campaign and per creator in one place, so you're not stitching together screenshots from five different apps to work out who actually sold something. If a creator's numbers stay flat after a fair run, that's the point to have a direct conversation about what's not working, which [how to renegotiate a creator deal that underperforms](/blog/renegotiate-underperforming-creator-deal) covers in more detail.

Set up a unique link or code for every creator in your next campaign before anyone posts, including the gifted ones. That single habit is the difference between a report full of views and a report you can actually use to decide who gets invited back.

faqs.a: You can, but you'll only learn whether the campaign worked overall, not which creator drove the sales. Unique codes per creator are the only way to compare performance between them.
faqs.q: Can I use the same discount code for every creator in a campaign?

faqs.a: Both work, and they do the same job of tying an order back to a specific creator. Codes are easier for a creator to say out loud in video content, while links suit written captions and bios better.
faqs.q: Do unique links work as well as discount codes for tracking sales?

faqs.a: Unique links and codes only capture sales that go through your tracked checkout flow, so in-store purchases influenced by a creator won't show up. For most ecommerce brands this is a small gap, but it's worth knowing the number you see is a floor, not the full picture.
faqs.q: What if a creator's followers buy in store instead of online?

faqs.a: Check within the first few days of the post going live. If there's no activity on the code at all, it's worth confirming the creator actually included it correctly before assuming the content simply isn't converting.
